extracted.intended_audience: lawyers, judges, and legal practitioners (administrative-law and labor-law litigators); law students
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and tests used by courts to evaluate the validity, scope, and deference due to administrative regulations and agency interpretations (e.g., Chevron, Auer, Mead, APA notice-and-comment) in the context of federal statutory delegation and regulatory conflicts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Chevron gap-filling and deference
rubrics_metrics.description: When an agency fills a congressional 'gap' reasonably, and in accordance with other applicable requirements, the courts accept the result as legally binding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites Chevron U.S.A., Inc. v. Natural Resources Defense Council, Inc., 467 U.S. 837, 843–844 (1984). Courts ask whether Congress explicitly addressed the precise question; if not, whether the agency's interpretation is based on a permissible construction of the statute. The opinion stresses that where the statute leaves gaps (e.g., scope/definition of terms) Congress authorized the agency to fill them and courts defer if the agency fills such gaps reasonably.

rubrics_metrics.name: Agency expertise and interstitial 'gap-filling' matters
rubrics_metrics.description: Matters concerning the definition and scope of statutory terms that are 'interstitial' (details Congress left to the agency) are appropriate subjects for agency rulemaking and expertise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If issue is one of detail within a broader definition entrusted to the agency, courts defer to agency’s considered judgment. The Court notes that satisfactory answers often require thorough knowledge and consultation the agency possesses (e.g., whether to include third-party-paid workers).

rubrics_metrics.name: Auer deference (agency interpretation of its own regulations)
rubrics_metrics.description: An agency’s interpretation of its own regulation is 'controlling' unless it is 'plainly erroneous or inconsistent with' the regulation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quoting Auer v. Robbins, 519 U.S. 452, 461 (1997). The Court applies this principle to the Department of Labor's interpretation of its two related regulations, concluding that the agency's interpretation of §552.109(a) as governing the third-party question is controlling so long as it is not plainly erroneous or inconsistent. The opinion also explains that an agency’s later-stated interpretation (e.g., in an advisory memorandum or brief) can reflect the agency's fair and considered judgment where the agency’s course of action indicates that.

rubrics_metrics.name: Skidmore persuasive-weight doctrine for interpretive rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Interpretive regulations may 'persuade' a reviewing court but do not necessarily 'bind' it; they receive weight according to their persuasiveness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites Skidmore v. Swift & Co., 323 U.S. 134 (1944) and Mead’s statement that interpretive rules enjoy no Chevron status 'as a class.' The Court distinguishes between interpretive rules (persuasive) and binding gap-filling rules (entitled to Chevron deference).

rubrics_metrics.name: Mead: interpretive rules and when Chevron applies
rubrics_metrics.description: Not all agency actions or rules automatically receive Chevron deference; whether an agency action does depends on factors such as Congress’s intent and the manner in which the agency acted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites United States v. Mead Corp., 533 U.S. 218 (2001). The opinion relies on Mead to explain that an agency's action that fills a statutory gap through formal procedures is more likely to be treated as a binding exercise of delegated authority, whereas purely interpretive rules 'enjoy no Chevron status as a class.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Factors suggesting Congress intended deference (single test list)
rubrics_metrics.description: Where an agency rule sets forth important individual rights and duties, the agency focuses fully upon the issue, uses full notice-and-comment procedures, the resulting rule falls within the statutory grant of authority, and the rule is reasonable, courts ordinarily assume Congress intended deference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The opinion lists these considerations as a unitary guide to determine whether courts should defer: (1) rule sets forth important individual rights and duties, (2) agency focused fully on the issue, (3) agency used full notice-and-comment procedures, (4) rule falls within the statutory grant of authority, and (5) the rule itself is reasonable. When present together they point toward Chevron-type deference (citing Mead and related cases).

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpretive vs. legislative rule status (notice-and-comment relevance)
rubrics_metrics.description: Interpretive rules (general statements of policy, or rules of agency organization/procedure) are typically exempt from APA notice-and-comment and, as a class, do not receive Chevron deference; legislative/rulemaking that affects rights/obligations and uses notice-and-comment is more likely to be treated as binding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 5 U.S.C. §553(b)(A) exempts interpretive rules from notice-and-comment. The opinion emphasizes that the Department used full notice-and-comment when promulgating §552.109(a), which is a strong indicator that the Department intended the rule to be a binding exercise of rulemaking authority rather than a mere interpretive statement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adequacy of notice under APA §553(b)(3) ('terms or substance' requirement)
rubrics_metrics.description: An agency must publish in its notice of proposed rulemaking either the terms or substance of the proposed rule or a description of the subjects and issues involved; the final rule must be a 'logical outgrowth' of the proposal to satisfy fair notice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites 5 U.S.C. §553(b)(3) and related case law requiring fair notice. The Courts of Appeals generally interpret this to mean the final rule must be a 'logical outgrowth' of the proposed rule (cases: National Black Media Coalition v. FCC; United Steelworkers v. Marshall; South Terminal Corp. v. EPA). The opinion applies this standard to the DOL's proceedings and finds the final rule (exempting all third-party companionship workers) was a reasonably foreseeable outcome of the notice and proposal process.

rubrics_metrics.name: Logical outgrowth / fair notice test
rubrics_metrics.description: The final adopted rule must be a 'logical outgrowth' of the proposed rule so that interested parties had fair opportunity to comment—i.e., final rule must not be an unforeseeable departure from the proposal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The opinion explains with examples that an agency's withdrawal or alteration of a proposed approach (and adoption of a different final rule) is permissible if the final result was reasonably foreseeable from the proposal. It cites cases (e.g., Arizona Public Serv. Co. v. EPA) to show notice sufficiency where the final rule differed but was within foreseeable outcomes of the proposal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specific controls over general in regulatory conflict
rubrics_metrics.description: When two agency regulations appear to conflict, the more specific regulation governing the particular issue ordinarily controls over a more general regulation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Court applies the principle that 'normally the specific governs the general' (citing Morales; Simpson) and reasons §552.109(a) (a third-party-specific 'Interpretation') is the more specific rule addressing how the companionship exemption applies to third-party employers, while §552.3 is a broader definitional regulation. Thus §552.109(a) governs the third-party-employment question.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contextual interpretation of overlapping regulations
rubrics_metrics.description: A court must examine regulatory context and history to determine which regulation was intended to address a specific question and whether apparent conflicts are truly inconsistent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The opinion looks to the structure, headings (Subpart A 'General Regulations' vs Subpart B 'Interpretations'), placement, and historical treatment to determine intent; Subpart B may contain detailed applications of Subpart A. Prior agency statements and practice are relevant but not dispositive; the Court examines purpose and administrative history to resolve the conflict.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of post-hoc agency explanations
rubrics_metrics.description: A later agency explanation (e.g., advisory memorandum or brief) is not automatically a suspect post-hoc rationalization if the agency’s course of action indicates that the interpretation reflects the agency's considered judgment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites Auer v. Robbins and Bowen v. Georgetown Univ. Hospital. The Court accepts that an agency’s formulation in an advisory memorandum or brief may be controlling where the agency has repeatedly considered the question and its actions indicate consistent, considered views—thus alleviating concerns of post-hoc rationalization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Change in agency interpretation and 'unfair surprise'
rubrics_metrics.description: A change in an agency’s interpretation does not by itself require disregard of the new interpretation so long as the change creates no unfair surprise to regulated parties and the agency used notice-and-comment when appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The opinion notes prior changes in DOL interpretations but finds that use of notice-and-comment rulemaking to codify interpretations makes unfair surprise unlikely; changes in interpretation are acceptable if properly promulgated and foreseeable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adequacy of agency explanation in final rule (sufficiency of reasoning)
rubrics_metrics.description: An agency must provide an adequate explanation for its final rule, but a reasonable and even brief explanation that was not objected to at the time may suffice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Court references the agency's explanation that exemptions can apply to third-party employers because such interpretation is 'more consistent' with statutory language and prior practices (40 Fed. Reg. 7405). It cites Global Crossing Telecommunications, Inc. v. Metrophones Telecommunications, Inc. for the proposition that a brief but reasonable explanation can be adequate decades later if not challenged at the time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assessment of whether regulation falls within statutory grant of authority
rubrics_metrics.description: A regulation must fall within the scope of authority granted by Congress for courts to treat it as an exercise of delegated rulemaking power entitled to deference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Court emphasizes Congress’s explicit authorization (e.g., 1974 Amendments authorizing Secretary of Labor 'to prescribe necessary rules, regulations, and orders') and treats that delegation as enabling DOL to define 'domestic service employment' and related terms; whether the agency stayed within that grant is a key review consideration under Chevron/Mead.
